text: All 27,702 surveyed species had prophage-associated eggNOG clusters (4,005,537 total). Packaging, lysis, and lysogenic regulation were near-universal; 34.9% of species carried all seven modules.
quote: All 27,702 species in the BERDL pangenome carry prophage-associated gene clusters, with 4,005,537 total prophage gene clusters identified via eggNOG annotations. Three modules are near-universal: packaging (A, 100%), lysis (D, 99.9%), and lysogenic regulation (F, 100%). The structurally variable modules — head morphogenesis (B, 56.1%), tail (C, 55.6%), and anti-defense (G, 64.3%) — show the most phylogenetic and environmental variation. 34.9% of species carry all 7 modules.
heading: 1. Prophage gene modules are universal but structurally variable across 27,702 bacterial species

text: The authors caution that near-universal modules may include domesticated, defective prophage remnants; head, tail, and anti-defense may better indicate more complete elements.
quote: Modules A, D, and F likely include many "domesticated" prophage remnants (Bobay et al. 2014) — defective prophages under purifying selection that retain packaging, lysis, and regulatory genes. The structurally variable modules (B, C, G) are more informative for understanding prophage ecology because their presence indicates more complete prophage elements.
heading: 1. Prophage gene modules are universal but structurally variable across 27,702 bacterial species

Mean contig co-localization across all tests is 0.769.

| D. Lysis | 13/15 | 4.45 | 0.901 | Strongest co-occurrence of any module |
| E. Integration | 1/15 | -1.93 | 0.420 | NOT co-occurring — expected for integrases |
| F. Lysogenic Regulation | 10/15 | 2.16 | 1.000 | Significant; perfect contig co-localization |

heading: Hypothesis Outcomes

text: The 27,702-species annotation result is not an intact-prophage prevalence estimate: individual associated clusters and domesticated remnants were counted. The report contrasts this with a cited ~46% genome estimate.
quote: The finding that **all 27,702 species carry prophage annotations** far exceeds Touchon et al.'s (2016) estimate that ~46% of bacterial genomes harbor prophages. This discrepancy likely reflects our broader definition: we identify individual prophage-associated gene clusters (including domesticated remnants), not intact prophages.
heading: Literature Context

text: As cited literature, Low et al. (2024) reported enrichment of prophage-encoded cargo genes in human-impacted environments across 38,605 genomes; this is not a measurement from the present project.
quote: 1. Low et al. (2024) demonstrated enrichment of prophage-encoded cargo genes in human-impacted environments across 38,605 genomes
heading: Literature Context

text: As cited literature, Tesson et al. (2024) reported that 89% of anti-defense systems localize in mobile genetic elements, predominantly prophages; this is not a measurement from the present project.
quote: 2. Tesson et al. (2024) found that 89% of anti-defense systems localize in mobile genetic elements, predominantly prophages
heading: Literature Context

text: Integration genes did not co-occur; the report relates this negative result to domesticated remnants that retain integrases.
quote: The finding that integration (E) genes do NOT co-occur is consistent with Bobay et al. (2014), who showed that domesticated prophage remnants — which are more common than intact prophages — often retain only integrases while losing the rest of the prophage backbone.
heading: Literature Context

text: Anti-defense genes had low co-localization (0.281); the report relates this to defense islands distinct from the core prophage.
quote: The low co-localization of anti-defense genes (G, 0.281) aligns with Pinilla-Redondo et al. (2020) and Rahimian et al. (2026), who found that anti-defense and defense systems co-localize into functional "defense islands" that are genomically distinct from the core prophage.
heading: Literature Context

text: No significant lineage-level environmental enrichment remained under permutations preserving host-family composition. The report contrasts this result with a published finding of viral habitat specificity.
quote: The lack of significant lineage-level enrichment (H1b) contrasts with Paez-Espino et al.'s (2016) finding of strong habitat-type specificity for most viral groups. However, our analysis used constrained permutations preserving host family composition — the lineage distribution is well-explained by host phylogeny alone, consistent with Mavrich & Hatfull (2017) showing that temperate phage evolution is primarily shaped by host range rather than environmental selection.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report describes a module-level analysis across >27,000 bacterial species and 10 environment categories; the priority claim is the authors' characterization.
quote: This study provides the first systematic, module-level analysis of prophage architecture across >27,000 bacterial species and 10 environment categories. Previous studies examined prophage presence/absence at the whole-prophage level (Touchon et al. 2016) or focused on specific phage types (Camarillo-Guerrero et al. 2021). Our module-level approach reveals that:
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Modules A, D, and F showed minimal environmental variation, whereas modules B, C, and G carried more environmental signal.
quote: 1. **Not all prophage functions respond equally to environment** — ubiquitous modules (A, D, F) show minimal environmental variation, while structurally variable modules (B, C, G) carry the environmental signal
heading: Novel Contribution

text: The summary calls anti-defense the most environmentally responsive module and reports human-associated enrichment and freshwater and animal-associated depletion. Its claim of the strongest human-associated enrichment conflicts with the report's earlier table: tail has log2(OR)=2.21, Z=10.86; head morphogenesis 1.98, 10.00; and anti-defense 1.70, 8.76. Anti-defense is not strongest by either listed measure.
quote: 2. **Anti-defense is the most environmentally responsive module** — showing the strongest enrichment (human-associated) and depletion (freshwater, animal-associated) signals
heading: Novel Contribution

text: The report finds module-level environmental effects beyond phylogeny but not lineage-level effects; modular exchange rather than whole-phage adaptation is its proposed interpretation.
quote: 3. **Module-level and lineage-level ecology are decoupled** — modules show environment effects beyond phylogeny, but lineages do not, suggesting modular exchange rather than whole-phage adaptation to environments
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Across 15 phyla, the report finds stronger linkage of packaging, lysis, and lysogenic-regulation genes and proposes a core-backbone/scattered-accessory model. Its phrase 'genomically independent' overstates the integration and anti-defense results: the earlier table reports significant co-occurrence in 1/15 and 3/11 tests, respectively, with mean contig co-localization of 0.420 and 0.281. These results indicate weaker co-occurrence and more scattered placement, not demonstrated independence.
quote: 4. **Empirical validation of prophage modularity at pangenome scale** — co-occurrence analysis across 15 phyla confirms that packaging, lysis, and lysogenic regulation genes behave as physically linked functional units, while integration and anti-defense genes are genomically independent, supporting a two-tier model of prophage organization (core backbone + scattered accessory functions)
heading: Novel Contribution

text: Prophage identification used eggNOG annotation proxies rather than dedicated detectors such as geNomad or VIBRANT. Domesticated remnants and bacterial homologs may inflate prevalence, and the false-positive rate is uncharacterized.
quote: 1. **Annotation-based prophage identification**: We use eggNOG functional annotations as proxies for prophage genes, not dedicated prophage detection tools (e.g., geNomad, VIBRANT). This likely inflates prophage prevalence by including domesticated remnants and bacterial homologs of phage genes (e.g., bacterial integrases). The false positive rate is uncharacterized.
heading: Limitations

text: Genome size was the dominant predictor of prophage burden (rho=0.717); stratification and partial correlations do not exclude residual confounding.
quote: 2. **Genome size confound**: Genome size is the dominant predictor of prophage burden (rho=0.717), and while we control for it via stratification and partial correlations, residual confounding cannot be excluded. Larger genomes have more genes of all types, not just prophage genes.
heading: Limitations

text: Sparse, inconsistent NCBI isolation_source metadata was collapsed into 10 categories; the "other_unknown" category contained 9,659 species (35%), limiting statistical power.
quote: 3. **Environment classification granularity**: NCBI isolation_source metadata is sparse and inconsistently labeled. Our classification into 10 categories collapses substantial within-category variation. The "other_unknown" category (9,659 species, 35%) limits statistical power.
heading: Limitations

text: NMDC prophage burden was inferred indirectly from taxonomy under an assumption of genus-level conservation. The approach has not been independently validated for prophage genes.
quote: 4. **NMDC inference is indirect**: Taxonomy-based prophage burden inference assumes genus-level conservation of prophage content, which may not hold for recently acquired or lost prophages. This approach was validated for the PHB granule ecology project but has not been independently validated for prophage genes.
heading: Limitations

text: Co-occurrence testing covered 15 species, one per phylum, with limited within-phylum replication. Head morphogenesis (B) was testable in only 6 species, and 200 null permutations limited z-score precision.
quote: 5. **Module co-occurrence scope**: NB03 tested 15 species (one per phylum), which provides broad phylogenetic coverage but limited within-phylum replication. Head morphogenesis (B) was testable in only 6 species due to sparsity. The 200-permutation null model provides adequate but not exhaustive precision for z-score estimation.
heading: Limitations

text: AlphaEarth environmental embeddings were available for only 28% of genomes, biasing the subsample toward better-sampled lineages.
quote: 6. **AlphaEarth embeddings**: Only 28% of genomes have environmental embeddings, creating a biased subsample toward clinically and environmentally well-sampled lineages.
heading: Limitations
